'''Stress resultants''' are simplified representations of the [[Cauchy stress tensor|stress]] state in [[structural element]]s such as [[beam theory|beams]], [[plate theory|plates]], or [[Plate theory|shells]].<ref>{{cite book |title= Introduction to composite materials design |last=Barbero |first=Ever J. |year=2010 |publisher=CRC Press |location=Boca Raton, FL |isbn=978-1-4200-7915-9 |url=http://www.crcpress.com/product/isbn/9781420079159 }}</ref>  The geometry of typical structural elements allows the internal stress state to be simplified because of the existence of a "thickness'" direction in which the size of the element is much smaller than in other directions.  As a consequence the three [[surface traction|traction]] components that vary from point to point in a cross-section can be replaced with a set of [[resultant force]]s and resultant moments.  These are the '''stress resultants''' (also called ''[[membrane force]]s'', ''[[shear force]]s'', and ''[[bending moment]]'') that may be used to determine the detailed stress state in the structural element.   A three-dimensional problem can then be reduced to a one-dimensional problem (for beams) or a two-dimensional problem (for plates and shells).

Stress resultants are defined as integrals of stress over the thickness of a structural element.  The integrals are weighted by integer powers the thickness coordinate ''z'' (or ''x''<sub>3</sub>). Stress resultants are so defined to represent the effect of stress as a membrane force ''N'' (zero power in ''z''), bending moment ''M'' (power 1) on a beam or [[shell (structure)]].  Stress resultants are necessary to eliminate the ''z'' dependency of the stress from the equations of the theory of plates and shells.

== Stress resultants in beams ==
[[Image:Components stress tensor cartesian.svg|370px|right|thumb|Components of stress on the surfaces of a structural element.]]
Consider the element shown in the adjacent figure.  Assume that the thickness direction is ''x''<sub>3</sub>.  If the element has been extracted from a beam, the width and thickness are comparable in size.  Let ''x''<sub>2</sub> be the width direction.  Then ''x''<sub>1</sub> is the length direction.

=== Membrane and shear forces ===
The resultant force vector due to the traction in the cross-section (''A'') perpendicular to the ''x''<sub>1</sub> axis is
:<math>
   \mathbf{F}_1 = \int_A (\sigma_{11} \mathbf{e}_1 + \sigma_{12} \mathbf{e}_2 + \sigma_{13} \mathbf{e}_3)\, dA
 </math>
where '''e'''<sub>1</sub>, '''e'''<sub>2</sub>, '''e'''<sub>3</sub> are the unit vectors along ''x''<sub>1</sub>, ''x''<sub>2</sub>, and ''x''<sub>3</sub>, respectively.  We define the stress resultants such that
:<math>
   \mathbf{F}_1 =: N_{11}\mathbf{e}_1 + V_2\mathbf{e}_2 + V_3\mathbf{e}_3 
 </math>
where ''N''<sub>11</sub> is the ''membrane force'' and ''V''<sub>2</sub>, ''V''<sub>3</sub> are the shear forces.  More explicitly, for a beam of height ''t'' and width ''b'', 
:<math>
    N_{11} = \int_{-b/2}^{b/2} \int_{-t/2}^{t/2} \sigma_{11}\,dx_3\,dx_2 \,.
 </math>
Similarly the shear force resultants are
:<math>
    \begin{bmatrix} V_2 \\ V_3 \end{bmatrix} =  \int_{-b/2}^{b/2} \int_{-t/2}^{t/2} 
         \begin{bmatrix} \sigma_{12} \\ \sigma_{13} \end{bmatrix} \,dx_3\,dx_2 \,.
 </math>

=== Bending moments ===
The bending moment vector due to stresses in the cross-section ''A'' perpendicular to the ''x''<sub>1</sub>-axis is given by
:<math>
   \mathbf{M}_1 = \int_A \mathbf{r} \times (\sigma_{11} \mathbf{e}_1 + \sigma_{12} \mathbf{e}_2 + \sigma_{13} \mathbf{e}_3)\, dA 
   \quad \text{where} \quad 
    \mathbf{r} = x_2\,\mathbf{e}_2 + x_3\,\mathbf{e}_3 \,.
 </math> 
Expanding this expression we have,
:<math>
   \mathbf{M}_1 = \int_A \left(-x_2\sigma_{11}\mathbf{e}_3 + x_2\sigma_{13}\mathbf{e}_1 + x_3\sigma_{11}\mathbf{e}_2 - x_3\sigma_{12}\mathbf{e}_1\right)dA =: M_{11}\,\mathbf{e}_1 + M_{12}\,\mathbf{e}_2 + M_{13}\,\mathbf{e}_3\,.
 </math>
We can write the bending moment resultant components as 
:<math>
  \begin{bmatrix} M_{11} \\ M_{12} \\M_{13} \end{bmatrix}
    := \int_{-b/2}^{b/2} \int_{-t/2}^{t/2} \begin{bmatrix} x_2\sigma_{13} - x_3\sigma_{12} \\ x_3\sigma_{11} \\ -x_2\sigma_{11} \end{bmatrix}\,dx_3\,dx_2 \,.
 </math>

== Stress resultants in plates and shells ==
For plates and shells, the ''x''<sub>1</sub> and ''x''<sub>2</sub> dimensions are much larger than the size in the ''x''<sub>3</sub> direction.  Integration over the area of cross-section would have to include one of the larger dimensions and would lead to a model that is too simple for practical calculations.  For this reason the stresses are only integrated through the thickness and the stress resultants are typically expressed in units of force ''per unit length'' (or moment ''per unit length'') instead of the true force and moment as is the case for beams.

=== Membrane  and shear forces ===
For plates and shells we have to consider two cross-sections.  The first is perpendicular to the ''x''<sub>1</sub> axis and the second is perpendicular to the ''x''<sub>2</sub> axis.  Following the same procedure as for beams, and keeping in mind that the resultants are now per unit length, we have
:<math>
   \mathbf{F}_1 = \int_{-t/2}^{t/2} (\sigma_{11} \mathbf{e}_1 + \sigma_{12} \mathbf{e}_2 + \sigma_{13} \mathbf{e}_3)\, dx_3
   \quad \text{and} \quad
   \mathbf{F}_2 = \int_{-t/2}^{t/2} (\sigma_{12} \mathbf{e}_1 + \sigma_{22} \mathbf{e}_2 + \sigma_{23} \mathbf{e}_3)\, dx_3
 </math>
We can write the above as
:<math>
   \mathbf{F}_1 = N_{11} \mathbf{e}_1 + N_{12} \mathbf{e}_2 + V_1  \mathbf{e}_3 \quad \text{and} \quad
   \mathbf{F}_2 = N_{12} \mathbf{e}_1 + N_{22} \mathbf{e}_2 + V_2  \mathbf{e}_3 
 </math>
where the membrane forces are defined as
:<math>
  \begin{bmatrix} N_{11} \\ N_{22} \\ N_{12} \end{bmatrix} := \int_{-t/2}^{t/2}
      \begin{bmatrix} \sigma_{11} \\ \sigma_{22} \\ \sigma_{12} \end{bmatrix}\, dx_3 
</math>
and the shear forces are defined as
:<math>
  \begin{bmatrix} V_1 \\ V_2 \end{bmatrix} = \int_{-t/2}^{t/2} \begin{bmatrix} \sigma_{13} \\ \sigma_{23} \end{bmatrix}\, dx_3 \,.
</math>

=== Bending moments ===
For the bending moment resultants, we have
:<math>
   \mathbf{M}_1 = \int_{-t/2}^{t/2} \mathbf{r} \times (\sigma_{11} \mathbf{e}_1 + \sigma_{12} \mathbf{e}_2 + \sigma_{13} \mathbf{e}_3)\, dx_3 
   \quad \text{and} \quad 
   \mathbf{M}_2 = \int_{-t/2}^{t/2} \mathbf{r} \times (\sigma_{12} \mathbf{e}_1 + \sigma_{22} \mathbf{e}_2 + \sigma_{23} \mathbf{e}_3)\, dx_3 
 </math>
where '''r''' = ''x''<sub>3</sub> '''e'''<sub>3</sub>.
Expanding these expressions we have,
:<math>
   \mathbf{M}_1 = \int_{-t/2}^{t/2} [-x_3\sigma_{12}\mathbf{e}_1 + x_3\sigma_{11}\mathbf{e}_2] \,dx_3
   \quad \text{and} \quad 
   \mathbf{M}_2 = \int_{-t/2}^{t/2} [-x_3\sigma_{22}\mathbf{e}_1 + x_3\sigma_{12}\mathbf{e}_2 ]\, dx_3
 </math>
Define the bending moment resultants such that
:<math>
  \mathbf{M}_1  =: -M_{12}\mathbf{e}_1 + M_{11}\mathbf{e}_2\quad \text{and} \quad
  \mathbf{M}_2 =: -M_{22}\mathbf{e}_1 + M_{12}\mathbf{e}_2 \,.
 </math>
Then, the bending moment resultants are given by
:<math>
  \begin{bmatrix} M_{11} \\ M_{22} \\ M_{12} \end{bmatrix} := \int_{-t/2}^{t/2} x_3 \,\begin{bmatrix} \sigma_{11} \\ \sigma_{22} \\ \sigma_{12} \end{bmatrix}\, dx_3 \,.
</math>
These are the resultants that are often found in the literature but care has to be taken to make sure that the signs are correctly interpreted.
